title: How story-video turns a spec into a video
note: Asha is an illustrative composite developer, not a real person. Everything shown is drawn from the story-video design spec itself.

scenes.heading: Turning a spec into a video
scenes.sub: One hand-drawn run cost 190k tokens and 22 minutes

right.label: The scripted kit: layouts filled from data

slots.footer: This walkthrough is about the story-video skill itself.

scenes.narration: Meet Asha, a developer who needs a narrated video from a design document, with nobody free to animate it by hand. The first run of this pipeline was done by hand, and drawing and reviewing fourteen slides cost about 190,000 tokens, seventy seven tool calls, and twenty two minutes. This is the scripted kit built to make that cheap and repeatable.
scenes.source: Why the design looks like this

scenes.heading: Five scripts, no drawing by hand
scenes.narration: Once Asha approves the storyboard, five scripts run in order, with no manual drawing. Setup installs ffmpeg and edge-tts into a private tools folder, never touching the system. Render-slides turns each scene into an HTML file from the layout kit, and render-frames screenshots every slide with a headless browser. Narrate voices the script, then build-video stitches it all into one finished file.

scenes.heading: What the hand-drawn run cost
scenes.sub: 77 tool calls and 22 minutes for 14 slides

stages.label: Tokens spent drawing slides by hand
Tool calls made along the way

scenes.narration: The pipeline was run once by hand, just to measure its real cost. Drawing and reviewing fourteen slides burned about one hundred ninety thousand tokens across seventy seven separate tool calls, and still took twenty two minutes. The slides themselves were only about sixty seven kilobytes of plain HTML, so turn count and image review were the true cost, not the drawing itself.
scenes.source: Why the design looks like this

scenes.heading: Stills and voice, not animation
scenes.sub: No animation between slides, no background music

cards.label: Still frames plus one clear voice

scenes.narration: This skill produces a narrated slideshow with fades between still frames, not an animated video, and the skill's own description says so plainly. Animation between slides was ruled out on purpose, and so was any background music track. What stays is simple: one clear still frame per scene, paired with one steady narrated voice, the same shape that proved itself in the reference run.
scenes.source: Goal; Decisions table (Slides, Out of scope)

scenes.heading: The validator catches mistakes first
scenes.sub: Every scene is checked before a build ever starts

items.label: Unknown icons and mismatched slots get rejected
Scene ids are two digits and always count upward
Each narration runs between 25 and 110 words
A narration sentence copied straight onto a slide

scenes.narration: Before any video gets built, a validator script checks every scene against a fixed set of rules. Icon names must be ones the pictogram kit recognizes, and every slide's slots must match its layout's own schema. Scene ids must be two digits and always count upward, never repeat. A sentence copied straight from the narration onto a slide gets caught and refused.

scenes.heading: Consent before any audio leaves
scenes.sub: Neural voice online, or a local voice offline

messages.text: Build with the neural voice, or keep everything local?
Neural voice, nothing sensitive in this walkthrough.

scenes.narration: Before any audio leaves the machine, the skill asks one plain question and waits for an answer. It offers the neural voice, which sends narration text to Microsoft's speech service with no licence or uptime guarantee, or the local OS voice, which never leaves the computer but sounds more robotic. Asha picks the neural voice, since this walkthrough has nothing sensitive to protect.
scenes.source: Phase 3: approve storyboard, consent to audio (G2)

scenes.heading: What gets committed, what stays local
scenes.sub: Frames, audio and segments are working files only
scenes.narration: Everything the pipeline writes lands under docs, story, and the slug name, inside the target project. The storyboard file, the slide sources, the finished MP4 and its subtitle file all get committed to the repository. The frames, audio and segment folders stay as working files, listed in a generated gitignore so nobody accidentally commits gigabytes of PNGs and MP3s.
scenes.source: Output layout in the target project

scenes.heading: One contact sheet, looked at once
scenes.sub: Look once; open a frame only if it looks wrong

panels.title: Open one only if it looks wrong

scenes.narration: Before Asha trusts a build, every rendered frame gets checked at once instead of one at a time. Build-video tiles every frame into a single contact sheet image, and Asha looks at that one picture rather than opening every frame one at a time. Only when a tile looks wrong does Asha open the full frame, fix the slot, and rerun the incremental steps.

scenes.heading: Voice today, and one voice not yet built
scenes.sub: Azure AI Speech is named but not implemented

phases.label: Not yet: a licensed voice
items: Azure AI Speech for client work

scenes.narration: Two voice options already ship today. The neural voice talks to Microsoft's edge-tts service, an unofficial route with no licence or uptime guarantee, while the local OS voice keeps everything on the machine but sounds robotic. For client-facing videos, the design names a third path, Azure AI Speech, a licensed route. It is only named, not implemented, so this scene stays marked planned.

scenes.heading: What stays out of every build
scenes.sub: No burn-in, no translation, no Azure integration
scenes.visual: A single video frame thumbnail with three small crossed-out badges beside it: subtitle text baked into the picture, a globe standing for translation, and a cloud standing for Azure, none of which the pictogram kit or any layout can draw.
scenes.narration: Three things stay out of this build entirely. Subtitles never get burned into the picture; they only ship as a separate dot srt file next to the video. There is no built-in way to translate narration into another language. Azure integration, the licensed alternative, is not wired into the pipeline either. No kit layout draws crossed-out globes or clouds, so an agent draws this scene by hand.
scenes.source: Decisions table (Subtitles, Voice, Out of scope)
